Minimum Risk Point Estimation of an Exponential Mean

Source: R/seq_mr_exp_mean.R
seq_mr_exp_mean.Rd

Given the data collected so far, checks the stopping rule of the purely sequential minimum risk point estimation (MRPE) procedure for the mean of an exponential population, such as a mean waiting time or time to failure (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009). Estimation error and sampling both cost something; the procedure looks for the sample size at which their expected total, the risk, is smallest. That sample size depends on the unknown mean, so observations are collected until the sample size reaches the size the current estimate calls for. The procedure is risk based, so there is no confidence level.

Usage

seq_mr_exp_mean(x, A, c, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of the observations collected so far (at least 1). All values must be positive.

A

The loss constant: the price of one unit of squared estimation error, in the same currency as c. A positive number.

c

The cost of sampling one observation. A positive number.

na.rm

Logical; should NA values be removed first? Default TRUE. With FALSE, missing values are an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and these rows:

mean

The sample mean, the point estimate.

risk

The estimated risk at the current sample size, \(A\bar{X}_n^2/n + c\,n\).

optimal_n

The sample size the current estimate of the mean calls for, \(\lceil (A/c)^{1/2}\,\bar{X}_n \rceil\).

current_n

The number of observations used.

Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE once current_n is at least optimal_n), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), method, loss_A, cost_c, and notes. conf_level and width are NULL.

Details

The function does not collect data and keeps no state. Call it after each new observation (or batch), starting once seq_mr_exp_mean_pilot observations are in hand, and stop sampling the first time attr(out, "is_satisfied") is TRUE.

The loss from estimating the mean \(\lambda\) by the sample mean of \(n\) observations is \(A(\bar{X}_n - \lambda)^2 + c\,n\): \(A\) prices a unit of squared estimation error and \(c\) is the cost of one observation. For exponential data the variance of the sample mean is \(\lambda^2/n\), so the risk for a fixed \(n\) is \(A\lambda^2/n + c\,n\), which is smallest at \(n^* = (A/c)^{1/2}\lambda\), where it equals \(2 c\,n^*\). The sequential rule replaces \(\lambda\) by the sample mean: sampling stops at the first \(n\) (at or beyond the pilot size) with $$n \ge (A/c)^{1/2}\,\bar{X}_n .$$ The optimal_n row is the right hand side rounded up, and the risk row is the estimated risk at the current sample size, \(A\bar{X}_n^2/n + c\,n\); both are evaluated at the current data.

The optimality is asymptotic. As the cost per observation falls (so that \(n^*\) grows), the expected final sample size approaches \(n^*\) and the risk of the procedure approaches the minimum \(2 c\,n^*\). When \(n^*\) is small the risk is noticeably above the minimum, more so than for a normal mean, because the sample mean of skewed data is itself the estimate of spread and a low early mean stops the sampling. In simulation (exponential data, the pilot of seq_mr_exp_mean_pilot() with its defaults, 40,000 replications, Monte Carlo standard error at most 0.006), with a mean of 1 the ratio of the risk to the minimum was 1.08, 1.16, 1.15, 1.05, and 1.02 when \(n^*\) was 10, 15, 20, 50, and 100 (that is, when \(A/c\) was 100, 225, 400, 2,500, and 10,000, for which the pilot is 4, 4, 5, 8, and 10). The ratio is not a function of \(n^*\) alone: the pilot depends only on \(A/c\), so the same \(n^*\) reached with another mean starts from a different pilot. With a mean of 0.25 (pilots of 7 to 20) the five ratios were 0.95, 1.04, 1.07, 1.04, and 1.01, and with a mean of 4 (pilots of 4 or 5) they were 1.08, 1.16, 1.16, 1.06, and 1.02. (A ratio below 1 is possible because the final sample size depends on the data.)

Data. The exponential model is for positive data. Zero or negative values are an error: they are not possible under the model, and a negative sample mean would give a negative sample size.

References

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

seq_mr_exp_mean_pilot; ts_br_exp_mean for two stage bounded risk estimation of the same mean; seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb, which makes no distributional assumption.

Other seq_mr_exp_mean: seq_mr_exp_mean_pilot()

Author

Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in, Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Mean time to resolve a support ticket, in minutes. An error of one
# minute (squared) is valued at 100 dollars and timing one more ticket
# costs 0.04 dollars. Times are simulated here with a mean of 6
# minutes, so the best sample size is sqrt(100 / 0.04) * 6 = 300.
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_mr_exp_mean_pilot(A = 100, c = 0.04)
minutes <- rexp(m, rate = 1 / 6)
out <- seq_mr_exp_mean(minutes, A = 100, c = 0.04)
out
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (exponential mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 8
#>   Criterion n     : 233
#> 
#>   mean              : 4.642232
#>   risk              : 269.699
#>   optimal_n         : 233
#>   current_n         : 8
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# Add one ticket at a time until the stopping rule is met.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  minutes <- c(minutes, rexp(1, rate = 1 / 6))
  out <- seq_mr_exp_mean(minutes, A = 100, c = 0.04)
}
out
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (exponential mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 295
#>   Criterion n     : 295
#> 
#>   mean              : 5.897602
#>   risk              : 23.59041
#>   optimal_n         : 295
#>   current_n         : 295
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
